items.title: Give the description a clause of its own

states.label: Describing verb
states.note: The describing verb follows the noun directly.

states.label: Describing clause
states.en: the water that is very deep
states.note: The particle *e* opens a whole describing clause. The word *tele* also adds very.

items.caption: The particle changes the structure; the added *tele* changes the degree. The water pair shows both differences without changing the noun.

items.title: An empty spot or a pointing-back word?

bins.label: A pointing-back word holds the spot

items.sm: ʻO le tama sā moe ʻi le fale.
items.en: The boy who slept in the house.
items.why: The boy is the one who slept; no word inside the clause stands for him.

items.sm: le meaʻai ʻua maua e le teine
items.why: The food is the thing acted on, and its spot stays empty.

items.sm: ʻO le aso sā siva ai le teine.
items.why: The pointing-back word *ai* holds the time’s spot.

items.sm: le fue na taufi aʻi le umu
items.en: the liana the food in the oven was covered with
items.why: *Aʻi* is the dedicated shape for what the action was done with; *ai* is heard in that job too.

items.sm: ʻO le mea sā alu atu le teine ʻi ai.
items.en: The place where the girl went to.
items.why: The pair *ʻi ai* is the usual shape for the place a movement is aimed at.

items.intro: Find how the clause shows the job of the person or thing named in front.

items.title: A person described without a noun

states.label: One particular person
states.note: The one-who word joins the specific article as *lē*. This example is in the past.

states.label: More than one
states.note: The one-who word stands on its own. This example uses the general particle.

states.label: The two words run together
states.note: With the general particle, one *e* can do both jobs.

items.caption: No noun names the people. The one-who word stands in that position and the clause describes them.
